title: Animal Physiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L animal physiology curriculum: cell physiology and membrane transport, nerve and muscle physiology, circulatory and respiratory physiology, digestive physiology, excretory physiology and osmoregulation, endocrine physiology, and thermoregulation, drawing on comparative examples across animal taxa.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is primarily established and maintained by:
options: The sodium-potassium (Na+/K+) pump and differential membrane permeability to ions
Active transport of glucose across the membrane
Osmotic movement of water alone
Diffusion of oxygen across the membrane
questions.correct_answer: The sodium-potassium (Na+/K+) pump and differential membrane permeability to ions
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+ ATPase pump actively maintains ion gradients (pumping 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in), and the membrane's greater resting permeability to K+ establishes the negative resting potential, typically around -70mV.

questions.question: During the depolarization phase of an action potential, which ion channels open first, allowing rapid influx of ions?
options: Voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels
Voltage-gated potassium (K+) channels
Calcium leak channels
Chloride channels
questions.correct_answer: Voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels
questions.explanation: Depolarization begins when voltage-gated Na+ channels open, allowing a rapid influx of Na+ ions that drives the membrane potential toward positive values.

questions.question: The 'all-or-none' principle of action potentials states that:
options: Once threshold is reached, an action potential fires at full amplitude regardless of further stimulus strength
Stronger stimuli always produce larger action potentials
Action potentials can be partially fired
Threshold has no effect on firing
questions.correct_answer: Once threshold is reached, an action potential fires at full amplitude regardless of further stimulus strength
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none events: if the depolarization reaches threshold, a full action potential fires; stimulus intensity is instead encoded by firing frequency, not amplitude.

questions.question: At a chemical synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic terminal triggers:
options: Influx of calcium ions, causing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter
Direct electrical flow of current into the postsynaptic cell
Immediate destruction of the synaptic vesicles
Reversal of the resting potential permanently
questions.correct_answer: Influx of calcium ions, causing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter
questions.explanation: Depolarization of the presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; the resulting calcium influx triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft.

questions.question: The sliding filament theory of muscle contraction explains that shortening of a sarcomere occurs because:
options: Actin and myosin filaments slide past each other without the filaments themselves shortening
The actin and myosin filaments each shorten in length
Only the myosin filaments contract
The sarcomere is destroyed and rebuilt with each contraction
questions.correct_answer: Actin and myosin filaments slide past each other without the filaments themselves shortening
questions.explanation: In the sliding filament model, myosin cross-bridges pull the actin filaments inward, sliding them past the myosin without any change in the length of the individual filaments themselves.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to which protein to initiate cross-bridge formation?
options: Troponin
Myosin light chain only
Titin
Actin directly, without any regulatory protein
questions.correct_answer: Troponin
questions.explanation: Calcium binds to troponin, causing a conformational shift that moves tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling to begin.

questions.question: ATP is required in skeletal muscle contraction primarily for:
options: Both cross-bridge cycling (powering the myosin head) and detachment of myosin from actin
Only the initial contraction, with no further role
Breaking down troponin permanently
Producing calcium ions
questions.correct_answer: Both cross-bridge cycling (powering the myosin head) and detachment of myosin from actin
questions.explanation: ATP binding to myosin is required to detach it from actin after a power stroke, and its hydrolysis re-energizes the myosin head for the next cycle -- without ATP, muscles remain in rigor (as in rigor mortis).

questions.question: In the mammalian heart, the sinoatrial (SA) node is significant because it:
options: Acts as the natural pacemaker, initiating each heartbeat
Pumps blood directly into the aorta
Prevents blood from flowing backward into the atria
Produces red blood cells
questions.correct_answer: Acts as the natural pacemaker, initiating each heartbeat
questions.explanation: The SA node, located in the right atrium, spontaneously generates rhythmic electrical impulses that set the pace for the entire heartbeat, earning its designation as the natural pacemaker.

questions.question: Systole and diastole refer respectively to:
options: Contraction of the heart (ejecting blood) and relaxation of the heart (filling with blood)
Relaxation and contraction of the heart
Opening and closing of the aortic valve only
Blood entering and leaving the lungs
questions.correct_answer: Contraction of the heart (ejecting blood) and relaxation of the heart (filling with blood)
questions.explanation: Systole is the phase of ventricular contraction that ejects blood, while diastole is the relaxation phase during which the heart chambers fill with blood.

questions.question: Cardiac output is calculated as:
options: Heart rate x stroke volume
Heart rate divided by stroke volume
Heart rate + stroke volume
Stroke volume divided by body weight
questions.correct_answer: Heart rate x stroke volume
questions.explanation: Cardiac output (volume of blood pumped per minute) equals the heart rate (beats per minute) multiplied by the stroke volume (blood ejected per beat).

questions.question: If an animal has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL, what is its cardiac output?
options: 4900 mL/min
140 mL/min
700 mL/min
1 mL/min
questions.correct_answer: 4900 mL/min
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 beats/min x 70 mL/beat = 4900 mL/min.

questions.question: Hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen is reduced by increased temperature, increased CO2, and decreased pH -- a phenomenon known as:
options: The Bohr effect
The Fick principle
The Frank-Starling law
The Bainbridge reflex
questions.correct_answer: The Bohr effect
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect describes how a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (reduced affinity) occurs under conditions of high CO2, low pH, or high temperature, such as in actively metabolizing tissue -- facilitating oxygen release where it is most needed.

questions.question: In mammalian lungs, gas exchange between alveoli and blood occurs primarily by:
options: Simple diffusion along partial pressure gradients
Active transport requiring ATP
Bulk flow driven by muscular contraction
Osmosis of oxygen molecules
questions.correct_answer: Simple diffusion along partial pressure gradients
questions.explanation: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane by passive diffusion, driven by differences in their partial pressures between air and blood.

questions.question: The primary muscle responsible for driving inspiration (inhalation) in mammals is the:
options: Diaphragm
Trapezius
Cardiac muscle
Bicep
questions.correct_answer: Diaphragm
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm flattens it, expanding the thoracic cavity and lowering intrapulmonary pressure, which draws air into the lungs.

questions.question: The primary stimulus that drives the rate and depth of breathing in mammals under normal conditions is:
options: Rising blood CO2 levels (and the resulting drop in pH), detected by central chemoreceptors
Blood glucose concentration
Body temperature alone
Blood oxygen levels exclusively, under all conditions
questions.correct_answer: Rising blood CO2 levels (and the resulting drop in pH), detected by central chemoreceptors
questions.explanation: Under normal physiological conditions, central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond primarily to increased CO2 (via the resulting decrease in cerebrospinal fluid pH), which is the dominant drive for ventilation.

questions.question: Peristalsis in the digestive tract refers to:
options: Rhythmic, wave-like contractions of smooth muscle that propel food along the gut
The secretion of digestive enzymes
Absorption of nutrients in the small intestine
The breakdown of food by chewing
questions.correct_answer: Rhythmic, wave-like contractions of smooth muscle that propel food along the gut
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the coordinated, wave-like contraction and relaxation of circular and longitudinal smooth muscle that moves food through the digestive tract.

questions.question: The enzyme pepsin, secreted in the stomach, functions to:
options: Begin the breakdown of proteins into smaller peptides
Digest starch into simple sugars
Emulsify dietary fats
Absorb amino acids directly
questions.correct_answer: Begin the breakdown of proteins into smaller peptides
questions.explanation: Pepsin, activated from pepsinogen by stomach acid (HCl), is a protease that begins protein digestion in the acidic environment of the stomach.

questions.question: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, aids digestion by:
options: Emulsifying fats into smaller droplets to increase surface area for lipase action
Directly digesting proteins
Neutralizing all stomach acid before it enters the intestine
Producing digestive enzymes
questions.correct_answer: Emulsifying fats into smaller droplets to increase surface area for lipase action
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets, greatly increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase to hydrolyze triglycerides.

questions.question: Ruminant animals (e.g., cattle) are able to digest cellulose primarily because of:
options: Symbiotic microorganisms in specialized stomach chambers (e.g., the rumen) that produce cellulase
Their own endogenous cellulase enzyme
An extra-long small intestine alone
A four-chambered heart
questions.correct_answer: Symbiotic microorganisms in specialized stomach chambers (e.g., the rumen) that produce cellulase
questions.explanation: Ruminants lack their own cellulase but host symbiotic bacteria and protozoa in the rumen that ferment cellulose, breaking it down into usable nutrients.

questions.question: In the mammalian kidney nephron, the primary site of bulk filtration of blood plasma is the:
options: Glomerulus (within the Bowman's capsule)
Loop of Henle
Collecting duct
Ureter
questions.correct_answer: Glomerulus (within the Bowman's capsule)
questions.explanation: Blood is filtered under pressure across the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule, forming the filtrate that then passes through the rest of the nephron.

questions.question: The loop of Henle's primary physiological role is to:
options: Establish a concentration (osmotic) gradient in the renal medulla that enables water reabsorption
Filter blood plasma directly
Secrete hormones into the bloodstream
Store urine before excretion
questions.correct_answer: Establish a concentration (osmotic) gradient in the renal medulla that enables water reabsorption
questions.explanation: The countercurrent multiplier system of the loop of Henle creates a steep osmotic gradient in the medulla, which the collecting duct uses to reabsorb water and concentrate urine.

questions.question: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released by the posterior pituitary, acts on the kidney to:
options: Increase water reabsorption by increasing permeability of the collecting duct
Increase urine volume by decreasing water reabsorption
Stimulate the secretion of digestive enzymes
Directly filter the blood
questions.correct_answer: Increase water reabsorption by increasing permeability of the collecting duct
questions.explanation: ADH increases the number of aquaporin water channels in the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption and producing more concentrated urine, conserving body water.

questions.question: Marine bony fish, living in a hyperosmotic environment relative to their body fluids, must osmoregulate by:
options: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
Never drinking water and producing large volumes of dilute urine
Absorbing water through the skin only
Excreting large volumes of concentrated salt water urine as their main osmoregulatory strategy
questions.correct_answer: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
questions.explanation: Because marine fish tend to lose water osmotically to the surrounding seawater, they drink seawater to replace it and use specialized chloride cells in the gills to actively excrete the excess salt.

questions.question: Freshwater bony fish, in contrast to marine fish, must osmoregulate by:
options: Producing large volumes of dilute urine and actively absorbing salts through the gills
Drinking large amounts of water and excreting concentrated urine
Excreting salt through specialized skin glands
Avoiding all water intake
questions.correct_answer: Producing large volumes of dilute urine and actively absorbing salts through the gills
questions.explanation: Freshwater fish constantly gain water osmotically from their hypoosmotic environment, so they excrete large volumes of dilute urine while actively taking up salts through gill chloride cells.

questions.question: Insulin, secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, primarily functions to:
options: Lower blood glucose levels by promoting cellular uptake and storage of glucose
Raise blood glucose levels by promoting glycogen breakdown
Regulate calcium levels in the blood
Stimulate the thyroid gland
questions.correct_answer: Lower blood glucose levels by promoting cellular uptake and storage of glucose
questions.explanation: Insulin promotes glucose uptake into cells (especially muscle and adipose tissue) and stimulates glycogen synthesis in the liver, lowering blood glucose concentration.

questions.question: Glucagon, secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas, has which effect on blood glucose?
options: Raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver
Lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose storage
Has no effect on blood glucose
Stimulates insulin release directly
questions.correct_answer: Raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver
questions.explanation: Glucagon acts antagonistically to insulin, stimulating the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the bloodstream when blood sugar is low.

questions.question: Hormones are generally classified into two broad chemical categories based on their mechanism of action: steroid hormones and:
options: Peptide/protein (amino acid-derived) hormones
Carbohydrate hormones
Lipid-insoluble minerals
Nucleic acid hormones
questions.correct_answer: Peptide/protein (amino acid-derived) hormones
questions.explanation: Hormones are broadly categorized as lipid-soluble steroid hormones (which can cross the cell membrane to bind intracellular receptors) and water-soluble peptide/protein hormones (which bind cell-surface receptors).

questions.question: The hypothalamic-pituitary axis illustrates negative feedback regulation because:
options: Rising levels of a target gland hormone inhibit further release of the releasing and stimulating hormones upstream
Hormone levels increase indefinitely without regulation
The pituitary gland has no communication with the hypothalamus
Target gland hormones always stimulate further release of pituitary hormones
questions.correct_answer: Rising levels of a target gland hormone inhibit further release of the releasing and stimulating hormones upstream
questions.explanation: In classic negative feedback, elevated levels of a downstream hormone (e.g., thyroid hormone) suppress the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing further stimulation and maintaining hormonal homeostasis.

questions.question: Endothermic animals (e.g., mammals and birds) maintain a stable internal body temperature primarily through:
options: Internal metabolic heat production regulated by physiological mechanisms
Reliance solely on external environmental heat sources
Complete absence of any thermoregulatory mechanism
Seasonal hibernation only
questions.correct_answer: Internal metabolic heat production regulated by physiological mechanisms
questions.explanation: Endotherms generate and regulate heat internally via metabolism (e.g., through thermogenesis), maintaining a stable core temperature regardless of ambient conditions, unlike ectotherms.

questions.question: Vasodilation of peripheral blood vessels in response to heat helps an endotherm to:
options: Increase heat loss to the environment by bringing more warm blood near the skin surface
Conserve heat by reducing blood flow to the skin
Increase metabolic rate
Trigger shivering thermogenesis
questions.correct_answer: Increase heat loss to the environment by bringing more warm blood near the skin surface
questions.explanation: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin, promoting heat loss to the environment through radiation and convection, an important cooling mechanism.

questions.question: Shivering thermogenesis generates body heat through:
options: Rapid, involuntary skeletal muscle contractions that release heat as a byproduct of ATP use
Increased sweat gland activity
Vasodilation of skin blood vessels
Reduced metabolic rate
questions.correct_answer: Rapid, involuntary skeletal muscle contractions that release heat as a byproduct of ATP use
questions.explanation: Shivering involves rapid, repeated muscle contractions that are metabolically inefficient, generating substantial heat as a byproduct that helps raise or maintain core body temperature.

questions.question: Countercurrent heat exchange systems, found in the limbs of many endotherms (e.g., arctic mammals and birds), function to:
options: Minimize heat loss to the environment by transferring heat from outgoing arterial blood to incoming venous blood
Maximize heat loss from the extremities
Increase overall body temperature above normal
Eliminate the need for a circulatory system in the limbs
questions.correct_answer: Minimize heat loss to the environment by transferring heat from outgoing arterial blood to incoming venous blood
questions.explanation: In countercurrent heat exchangers, warm arterial blood flowing toward the extremities transfers heat to cooler venous blood returning to the body core, conserving core body heat while allowing the extremities to remain cooler.

questions.question: In active transport across cell membranes, molecules are moved:
options: Against their concentration gradient, using energy (typically ATP)
Down their concentration gradient without energy input
Only through simple diffusion
Exclusively via osmosis
questions.correct_answer: Against their concentration gradient, using energy (typically ATP)
questions.explanation: Active transport requires cellular energy expenditure (usually from ATP hydrolysis) to move molecules against their concentration gradient, unlike passive diffusion.

questions.question: Osmosis refers specifically to the movement of:
options: Water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration
Any solute molecules across a membrane
Ions only, via protein channels
Gases across a respiratory surface
questions.correct_answer: Water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water specifically, moving toward the side of a semi-permeable membrane with higher solute concentration (lower water potential).
